(general)") | The **Second English Civil War** took place between February and August 1648 in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") and [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales"). It forms part of the series of conflicts known collectively as the 1639–1653 [Wars of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Wars of the Three Kingdoms"), which include the 1641–1653 [Irish Confederate Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Confederate_Wars "Irish Confederate Wars"), the 1639–1640 [Bishops' Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops%27_Wars "Bishops' Wars"), and the 1649–1653 [Cromwellian conquest of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromwellian_conquest_of_Ireland "Cromwellian conquest of Ireland"). Following his defeat in the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War"), in May 1646 [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") surrendered to the Scots [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters"), rather than [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England"). By doing so, he hoped to exploit divisions between English and Scots [Presbyterians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_polity "Presbyterian polity"), and English [Independents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_/(religion/) "Independent (religion)"). At this stage, all parties expected Charles to continue as king, which combined with their internal divisions, allowed him to refuse significant concessions. When the Presbyterian majority in Parliament failed to disband the [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") in late 1647, many joined with the Scottish [Engagers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers "Engagers") in an agreement to restore Charles to the English throne. The [subsequent Scottish invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_invasion_of_England_/(1648/) "Scottish invasion of England (1648)") was supported by [Royalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier") risings in South Wales, Kent, Essex and Lancashire, along with sections of the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy"). However, these were poorly co-ordinated and by the end of August 1648, they had been defeated by forces under [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") and [Thomas Fairfax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Fairfax,_3rd_Lord_Fairfax_of_Cameron "Thomas Fairfax, 3rd Lord Fairfax of Cameron"). This led to the [execution of Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Execution_of_Charles_I "Execution of Charles I") in January 1649 and establishment of the [Commonwealth of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England "Commonwealth of England"), after which the Covenanters crowned his son [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") King of Scotland, leading to the 1650 to 1652 [Anglo-Scottish War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Scottish_war_/(1650%E2%80%931652/) "Anglo-Scottish war (1650–1652)"). [![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Denzil_Holles%2C_1st_Baron_Holles_of_Ifield.jpg/250px-Denzil_Holles%2C_1st_Baron_Holles_of_Ifield.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Denzil_Holles,_1st_Baron_Holles_of_Ifield.jpg) [Denzil Holles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denzil_Holles,_1st_Baron_Holles "Denzil Holles, 1st Baron Holles"), a leader of the [Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_polity "Presbyterian polity") faction in Parliament [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") ruled the three separate kingdoms of [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Scotland "Kingdom of Scotland"), [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Ireland "Kingdom of Ireland") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") in a [personal union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_union "Personal union"). Thus the conflicts that started in 1639 and lasted until 1653 are known as the [Wars of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Wars of the Three Kingdoms"). The 1639 and 1640 [Bishops' Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops%27_Wars "Bishops' Wars") began when Charles attempted to bring the [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland"), _[the Kirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_/(word/) "Kirk (word)")_, into line with reforms recently enacted within the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKenyonOhlmeyer200215%E2%80%9316-1) Known as [Laudianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laudianism "Laudianism"), these changes were opposed by English [Puritans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puritans "Puritans") and the vast majority of Scots, many of whom signed the [National Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Covenant "National Covenant") pledging to preserve the Kirk by force of arms. Known as [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters"), their victory in the Bishops' Wars confirmed their control of Scotland and provided momentum for the king's opponents in England. The Covenanters passed laws that required all civil office-holders, [MPs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Members_of_Parliament "Members of Parliament") and clerics to sign the Covenant, and gave the [Parliament of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Scotland "Parliament of Scotland") the right to approve all Royal councillors in Scotland.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStewart2016124%E2%80%93125-2) Tensions about religion and the governance of the nation were also rising in England. All parties agreed a 'well-ordered' monarchy was divinely mandated, but they disagreed on what 'well-ordered' meant, particularly with regards to the balance of power between king and parliament, and on the question of where ultimate authority in clerical affairs lay. [Royalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier") generally supported a [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England") governed by [bishops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_polity "Episcopal polity"), appointed by, and answerable to, the king; [Parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") tended to believe that church leaders should be appointed by their congregations. The relationship between Charles and his [English Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") eventually broke down entirely, resulting in the outbreak of the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") in 1642.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKenyonOhlmeyer200226%E2%80%9328,_32-3) In England, Charles's supporters, the [Royalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier"), were opposed by the combined forces of the [Parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") and the Scots. In 1643 the latter pair formed an alliance bound by the [Solemn League and Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solemn_League_and_Covenant "Solemn League and Covenant"), in which the English Parliament agreed to reform the English church along similar lines to the Scottish Kirk in return for the Scots' military assistance.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoolrych2002271-4) After four years of war the Royalists were defeated and Charles surrendered to the Scots on 5 May 1646.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoolrych2002329%E2%80%93330-5) The Scots agreed with the English Parliament on a peace settlement which would be put before the king. Known as the [Newcastle Propositions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heads_of_Proposals#Background_and_Newcastle_propositions "Heads of Proposals"), it would have required all the king's subjects in Scotland, England and Ireland to sign the Solemn League and Covenant, brought the church in each kingdom into accordance with the Covenant and with [Presbyterianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism "Presbyterianism"), and ceded much of Charles's secular authority as king of England to the English Parliament. The Scots spent some months trying to persuade Charles to agree to these terms, but he refused to do so. Under pressure from the English to withdraw their forces now the war was over, the Scots handed Charles over to the English Parliamentary forces in exchange for a financial settlement and left England on 3 February 1647.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoolrych2002340%E2%80%93349-6) [![Image 13](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Carisbrooke_Castle_from_south.jpg/250px-Carisbrooke_Castle_from_south.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carisbrooke_Castle_from_south.jpg) [Carisbrooke Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle"), on the Isle of Wight, where Charles was held in December 1648 In England, Parliament was struggling with the economic cost of the war, a poor 1646 harvest, and a recurrence of the plague. The moderate Presbyterian faction led by [Denzil Holles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denzil_Holles,_1st_Baron_Holles "Denzil Holles, 1st Baron Holles") dominated Parliament and was supported by the London [Trained Bands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trained_Bands "Trained Bands"), the Army of the Western Association, leaders like [Rowland Laugharne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowland_Laugharne "Rowland Laugharne") in Wales, and elements of the [English navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy"). By March 1647, the [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") was owed more than £3 million in unpaid wages;[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-8) Parliament ordered it to Ireland, stating only those who agreed to go would be paid. When their [representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agitators "Agitators") demanded full payment for all in advance, it was ordered that it be disbanded, but its leaders refused to do so.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTERees2016173%E2%80%93174-9) Charles now engaged in separate negotiations with different factions. Presbyterian English Parliamentarians and the Scots wanted him to accept a modified version of the Newcastle Propositions, but in June 1647, [Cornet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornet_/(rank/) "Cornet (rank)") [George Joyce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Joyce "George Joyce") of the New Model Army seized Charles,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoolrych2002364-10) and the [army council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_Council_/(1647/) "Army Council (1647)") pressed him to accept the [Heads of Proposals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heads_of_Proposals "Heads of Proposals"), a less demanding set of terms which, crucially, did not require a Presbyterian reformation of the church.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGentles2002144%E2%80%93150-11) On 26 July pro-Presbyterian rioters burst into Parliament, demanding that Charles be invited to London; fearing that the king might be restored without concessions, the New Model Army took control of the city in early August, while the Army Council re-established their authority over the rank and file by suppressing the [Corkbush Field mutiny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corkbush_Field_mutiny "Corkbush Field mutiny").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrayling201723-12) The [Eleven Members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleven_Members "Eleven Members") of Parliament whom the army identified as opposed to its interests were removed forcibly,[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-13) and on 20 August Oliver Cromwell brought a regiment of cavalry to Hyde Park, rode with an escort to Parliament and pushed through the [Null and Void Ordinance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Null_and_Void_Ordinance "Null and Void Ordinance"), leading to the Presbyterian MPs withdrawing from Parliament.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-14) Charles eventually rejected the Heads of Proposals, and instead signed an offer known as the [Engagement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers "Engagers"), which had been thrashed out with the Scottish delegation, on 26 December 1647. Charles agreed to confirm the Solemn League and Covenant by [Act of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Act_of_Parliament "Act of Parliament") in both kingdoms, and to accept Presbyterianism in England, but only for a trial period of three years, in return for the Scots' assistance in regaining his throne in England.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStewart2016258%E2%80%93259-15) When the delegation returned to Edinburgh with the Engagement, the Scots were bitterly divided on whether to [ratify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratification "Ratification") its terms. Its supporters, who became known as the Engagers, argued that it offered the best chance the Scots would get of acceptance of the Covenant across the three kingdoms, and that rejecting it risked pushing Charles to accept the Heads of Proposals. It was opposed by those who believed that to send an army into England on behalf of the king would be to break the Solemn League and Covenant, and that it offered no guarantee of a lasting Presbyterian church in England; the Kirk went so far as to issue a declaration on 5 May 1648 condemning the Engagement as a breach of God's law.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStewart2016258%E2%80%93261-16) After a protracted political struggle, the Engagers gained a majority in the Scottish Parliament, and it was accepted.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFurgol200264-17) Western England and South Wales; 1645 Wales was a sensitive area, since most of it had been Royalist during the war, while [Harlech Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlech_Castle "Harlech Castle") was the last of their strongpoints to surrender in March 1647. The interception of secret messages between Charles and the [Irish Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_Ireland "Confederate Ireland") made it important to secure ports like [Cardiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff "Cardiff") and [Milford Haven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford_Haven "Milford Haven") since they controlled shipping routes with Ireland. The [Army Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_Council_/(1647/) "Army Council (1647)") viewed the local commanders, [John Poyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Poyer "John Poyer") and [Rowland Laugharne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowland_Laugharne "Rowland Laugharne"), with suspicion, since they supported the Parliamentarian moderates. In July, Horton was sent to replace Laugharne, and secure these positions.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoberts2004-18) The revolt began in [Pembrokeshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire "Pembrokeshire"), an area controlled by Parliament since early 1643. Like their New Model colleagues, the soldiers had not been paid for months, and feared being disbanded without their wages. In early March, Poyer, Governor of [Pembroke Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembroke_Castle "Pembroke Castle"), refused to relinquish command; he was soon joined by [Rice Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice_Powell "Rice Powell"), who commanded [Tenby Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenby_Castle "Tenby Castle"), then by Laugharne.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2004431-19) What began as a dispute over pay turned political when the Welsh rebels made contact with Charles. Most Royalists had sworn not to bear arms against Parliament and did not participate, one exception being [Nicholas Kemeys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Kemeys "Nicholas Kemeys"), who held [Chepstow Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chepstow_Castle "Chepstow Castle") for the king. By the end of April, Laugharne had assembled around 8,000 troops, and was marching on [Cardiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff "Cardiff"), but was defeated at [St Fagans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_St_Fagans "Battle of St Fagans") on 8 May.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2004436-20) This ended the revolt as a serious threat, although Pembroke Castle did not surrender until 11 July, with a minor rising in [North Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Wales "North Wales") suppressed at [Y Dalar Hir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Y_Dalar_Hir "Battle of Y Dalar Hir") in June and [Anglesey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglesey "Anglesey") retaken from the rebels in early October. The Welsh rising is generally not considered part of a planned, Royalist plot, but largely accidental; however, its retention was vital for future operations in Ireland.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2004439%E2%80%93441-21) Revolt against Parliament in Kent --------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_English_Civil_War&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Revolt against Parliament in Kent")\] A precursor to [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent "Kent")'s Second Civil War had come on Wednesday, 22 December 1647, when [Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury "Canterbury")'s [town crier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_crier "Town crier") had proclaimed the county committee's order for the [suppression of Christmas Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suppression_of_Christmas_Day "Suppression of Christmas Day") and its treatment as any other working day.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-22)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrand1905117,_118-23) However, a large crowd gathered on Christmas to demand a church service, decorate doorways with holly bushes, and keep the shops shut. This crowd – under the slogan "For God, King Charles, and Kent" – then descended into violence and riot, with a soldier being assaulted, the mayor's house attacked, and the city under the rioters' control for several weeks until forced to surrender in early January.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurston1985-24) On 21 May 1648, Kent rose in revolt in the King's name, and a few days later a most serious blow to the Independents was struck by the defection of the Navy, from command of which they had removed Vice-Admiral [William Batten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Batten "William Batten"), as being a Presbyterian. Though a former Lord High Admiral, the [Earl of Warwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Rich,_2nd_Earl_of_Warwick "Robert Rich, 2nd Earl of Warwick"), also a Presbyterian, was brought back to the service, it was not long before the Navy made a purely Royalist declaration and placed itself under the command of the [Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"). But Fairfax had a clearer view and a clearer purpose than the distracted Parliament. He moved quickly into Kent, and on the evening of 1 June, [stormed Maidstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Maidstone "Battle of Maidstone") by open force, after which the local levies dispersed to their homes, and the more determined Royalists, after a futile attempt to induce the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London") to declare for them, fled into [Essex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essex "Essex").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191146._The_English_War-25) Before leaving for Essex, Fairfax delegated command of the Parliamentarian forces to Colonel [Nathaniel Rich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathaniel_Rich_/(soldier/) "Nathaniel Rich (soldier)") to deal with the remnants of the Kentish revolt in the east of the county, where the naval vessels in [the Downs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Downs_/(ship_anchorage/) "The Downs (ship anchorage)") had gone over to the Royalists and Royalist forces had taken control of the three previously Parliamentarian "castles of the Downs" ([Walmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walmer_Castle "Walmer Castle"), [Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deal_Castle "Deal Castle"), and [Sandown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandown_Castle,_Kent "Sandown Castle, Kent")) and were trying to take control of [Dover Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover_Castle "Dover Castle"). Rich arrived at Dover on 5 June 1648 and prevented the attempt, before moving to the Downs. He took almost a month to retake Walmer (15 June to 12 July), before moving on to Deal and Sandown castles. Even then, due to the small size of Rich's force, he was unable to surround both Sandown and Deal at once and the two garrisons were able to send help to each other. At Deal he was also under bombardment from the Royalist warships, which had arrived on 15 July but been prevented from landing reinforcements. On the 16th, thirty [Flemish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders") ships arrived with about 1500 [mercenaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercenary "Mercenary") and – though the ships soon left when the Royalists ran out of money to pay them – this incited sufficient Kentish fear of foreign invasion to allow [Michael Livesey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Livesey "Michael Livesey") to raise a large enough force to come to Colonel Rich's aid. On 28 July, the Royalist warships returned and, after three weeks of failed attempts to land a relief force at Deal, on the night of 13 August managed to land 800 soldiers and sailors under cover of darkness. This force might have been able to surprise the besieging Parliamentarian force from the rear had it not been for a Royalist deserter who alerted the besiegers in time to defeat the Royalists, with less than a hundred of them managing to get back to the ships (though 300 managed to flee to Sandown Castle). Another attempt at landing soon afterwards also failed and, when on 23 August news was fired into Deal Castle on an arrow of [Cromwell's victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#Battle_of_Preston) at [Preston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Preston_/(1648/) "Battle of Preston (1648)"), most Royalist hope was lost and two days later Deal's garrison surrendered, followed by Sandown on 5 September. This finally ended the Kentish rebellion. Rich was made Captain of Deal Castle, a position he held until 1653 and in which he spent around £500 on repairs.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-26) In [Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall "Cornwall"), [Northamptonshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northamptonshire "Northamptonshire"), [North Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Wales "North Wales"), and [Lincolnshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincolnshire "Lincolnshire") the revolt collapsed as easily as that in Kent. Only in [South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Wales "South Wales"), [Essex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essex "Essex"), and the north of England was there serious fighting. In the first of these districts, South Wales, Cromwell rapidly reduced all the fortresses except Pembroke. Here Laugharne, Poyer, and Powel held out with the desperate courage of deserters.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191146._The_English_War-25) [![Image 14](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Pontefract_Castle_1648.jpg/330px-Pontefract_Castle_1648.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pontefract_Castle_1648.jpg) Pontefract Castle in 1648, with civil war fortifications surrounding the old medieval ones. In the north, [Pontefract Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontefract_Castle "Pontefract Castle") was surprised by the Royalists, and shortly afterwards [Scarborough Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarborough_Castle "Scarborough Castle") declared for the King as well. Fairfax, after his success at Maidstone and the pacification of Kent, turned northward to reduce Essex, where, under their ardent, experienced, and popular leader [Charles Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lucas "Charles Lucas"), the Royalists were in arms in great numbers. Fairfax soon drove Lucas into [Colchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colchester "Colchester"), but the first attack on the town was repulsed and he had to settle down to a long and wearisome [siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Colchester "Siege of Colchester").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191146._The_English_War-25) A [Surrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrey "Surrey") rising is remembered for the death of the young and gallant [Lord Francis Villiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Villiers,_2nd_Duke_of_Buckingham "George Villiers, 2nd Duke of Buckingham"), younger brother of [George Villiers, 2nd Duke of Buckingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Villiers,_2nd_Duke_of_Buckingham "George Villiers, 2nd Duke of Buckingham"), in a skirmish at [Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_upon_Thames "Kingston upon Thames") (7 July 1648). The rising collapsed almost as soon as it had gathered force, and its leaders, the [Duke of Buckingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Villiers,_2nd_Duke_of_Buckingham "George Villiers, 2nd Duke of Buckingham") and Henry Rich, the [Earl of Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Rich,_1st_Earl_of_Holland "Henry Rich, 1st Earl of Holland"), escaped, after another attempt to induce London to declare for them, to [St Albans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Albans "St Albans") and [St Neots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Neots "St Neots"), where Holland was taken prisoner. Buckingham escaped overseas.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191146._The_English_War-25) Lambert in the north -------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_English_Civil_War&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Lambert in the north")\] Major-General [John Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lambert_/(general/) "John Lambert (general)"), a brilliant young Parliamentarian commander of twenty-nine, was more than equal to the situation. He left the sieges of [Pontefract Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontefract_Castle "Pontefract Castle") and [Scarborough Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarborough_Castle "Scarborough Castle") to Colonel [Edward Rossiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Rossiter "Edward Rossiter"), and hurried into [Cumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland,_England "Cumberland, England") to deal with the English Royalists under [Marmaduke Langdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marmaduke_Langdale "Marmaduke Langdale"). With his [cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalry "Cavalry"), Lambert got into touch with the enemy about [Carlisle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlisle,_Cumbria "Carlisle, Cumbria") and slowly fell back to [Bowes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowes "Bowes") and [Barnard Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnard_Castle "Barnard Castle"). Lambert fought small rearguard actions to annoy the enemy and gain time. Langdale did not follow him into the mountains. Instead, he occupied himself in gathering recruits, supplies of material, and food for the advancing Scots.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191147._Lambert_in_the_north-27) Lambert, reinforced from the Midlands, reappeared early in June and drove Langdale back to Carlisle with his work half finished. About the same time, the local cavalry of [Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham,_England "Durham, England") and [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland") were put into the field for the Parliamentarians by [Arthur Hesilrige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Hesilrige "Arthur Hesilrige"), governor of [Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne"). On 30 June, under the direct command of Colonel [Robert Lilburne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Lilburne "Robert Lilburne"), these mounted forces won a considerable success at the [River Coquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Coquet "River Coquet").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191147._Lambert_in_the_north-27) This reverse, coupled with the existence of Langdale's Royalist force on the Cumberland side, practically compelled [Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 1st Duke of Hamilton") to choose the west coast route for his advance. His Scottish [Engager](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engager "Engager") army began slowly to move down the long [couloir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Couloir "Couloir") between the mountains and the sea. The Campaign of Preston which followed is one of the most brilliant in English history.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191147._Lambert_in_the_north-27) Campaign of Preston ------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_English_Civil_War&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Campaign of Preston")\] On 8 July 1648, when the Scottish [Engager](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engager "Engager") army [crossed the Anglo–Scottish border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_invasion_of_England_/(1648/) "Scottish invasion of England (1648)") in support of the English Royalists,[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-28) the military situation was well defined. For the Parliamentarians, Cromwell besieged [Pembroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Pembroke "Siege of Pembroke") in West Wales, Fairfax besieged [Colchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Colchester "Siege of Colchester") in Essex, and Colonel Rossiter besieged [Pontefract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontefract "Pontefract") and [Scarborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarborough,_North_Yorkshire "Scarborough, North Yorkshire") in the north. On 11 July, Pembroke fell and Colchester followed on 28 August.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191147._Lambert_in_the_north-27) Elsewhere the rebellion, which had been put down by rapidity of action rather than sheer weight of numbers, smouldered, and [Charles, the Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"), with the fleet cruised along the Essex coast. Cromwell and Lambert, however, understood each other perfectly, while the Scottish commanders quarrelled with each other and with Langdale.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191148._Campaign_of_Preston-29) As the English uprisings were close to collapse, Royalist hopes centred on the Engager Scottish army. It was not the same veteran army of the [Earl of Leven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Leslie,_1st_Earl_of_Leven "Alexander Leslie, 1st Earl of Leven"), which had long been disbanded. For the most part it consisted of raw levies. The [Kirk party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_party "Kirk party") had refused to sanction [the Engagement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Engagement_/(1647/) "The Engagement (1647)") (an agreement between Charles I and the [Scots Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Scotland "Parliament of Scotland") for the Scots to intervene in England on behalf of Charles), causing [David Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leslie_/(Scottish_general/) "David Leslie (Scottish general)") and thousands of experienced officers and men to decline to serve. The leadership of the [Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 1st Duke of Hamilton") proved to be poor and his army was so ill provided for that as soon as England was invaded it began to plunder the countryside for sustenance.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191147._Lambert_in_the_north-27) On 8 July the Scots, with Langdale leading an advance guard, were near Carlisle, and reinforcements from [Ulster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster "Ulster") were expected daily. Lambert's cavalry were at [Penrith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrith,_Cumbria "Penrith, Cumbria"), [Hexham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexham "Hexham") and Newcastle, too weak to fight and having only skillful leading and rapidity of movement to enable them to gain time.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191148._Campaign_of_Preston-29) [Appleby Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleby-in-Westmorland "Appleby-in-Westmorland") surrendered to the Scots on 31 July, whereat Lambert, who was still hanging on to the flank of the Scottish advance, fell back from [Barnard Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnard_Castle "Barnard Castle") to [Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond,_North_Yorkshire "Richmond, North Yorkshire") so as to close [Wensleydale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wensleydale "Wensleydale") against any attempt of the invaders to march on [Pontefract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontefract "Pontefract"). All the restless energy of Langdale's cavalry were unable to dislodge Lambert from the passes or to find out what was behind that impenetrable cavalry screen. The crisis was now at hand. Cromwell had received the surrender of Pembroke Castle on 11 July, and had marched off, with his men unpaid, ragged and shoeless, at full speed through the Midlands. Rains and storms delayed his march, but he knew that the Duke of Hamilton in the broken ground of Westmorland was still worse off. Shoes from [Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northampton "Northampton") and stockings from [Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry "Coventry") met him at [Nottingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nottingham "Nottingham"), and gathering up the local levies as he went, he made for [Doncaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doncaster "Doncaster"), where he arrived on 8 August, having gained six days in advance of the time he had allowed himself for the march. He then called up artillery from [Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_upon_Hull "Kingston upon Hull"), exchanged his local levies for the regulars who were besieging Pontefract, and set off to meet Lambert. On 12 August he was at [Wetherby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wetherby "Wetherby"), Lambert at [Otley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otley "Otley"), Langdale at [Skipton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skipton "Skipton") and [Gargrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gargrave "Gargrave"), Hamilton at [Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster,_England "Lancaster, England"), and [George Monro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Munro,_1st_of_Newmore "George Munro, 1st of Newmore") with the Scots from Ulster and the Carlisle Royalists (organized as a separate command owing to friction between Monro and the generals of the main army) at [Hornby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hornby,_Lancashire "Hornby, Lancashire"). On 13 August, while Cromwell was marching to join Lambert at Otley, the Scottish leaders were still disputing whether they should make for Pontefract or continue through [Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire "Lancashire") so as to join [Lord Byron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Byron,_1st_Baron_Byron "John Byron, 1st Baron Byron") and the Cheshire Royalists.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191148._Campaign_of_Preston-29) On 14 August 1648 Cromwell and Lambert were at Skipton, on 15 August at [Gisburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gisburn "Gisburn"), and on 16 August they marched down the valley of the [Ribble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Ribble "River Ribble") towards [Preston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preston,_Lancashire "Preston, Lancashire") with full knowledge of the enemy's dispositions and full determination to attack him. They had with them troops from both the Army and the militias of [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire"), Durham, Northumberland and Lancashire, and were heavily outnumbered, having only 8,600 men against perhaps 20,000 of Hamilton's command. But the latter were scattered for convenience of supply along the road from Lancaster, through Preston, towards [Wigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wigan "Wigan"), Langdale's corps having thus become the left flank guard instead of the advanced guard.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191149._Preston_Fight-30) Langdale called in his advanced parties, perhaps with a view to resuming the duties of advanced guard, on the night of 13 August, and collected them near [Longridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longridge "Longridge"). It is not clear whether he reported Cromwell's advance, but, if he did, Hamilton ignored the report, for on 17 August Monro was half a day's march to the north, Langdale east of Preston, and the main army strung out on the Wigan road, Major-General [William Baillie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Baillie_/(soldier/) "William Baillie (soldier)") with a body of foot, the rear of the column, being still in Preston. Hamilton, yielding to the importunity of his lieutenant-general, [James Livingston, 1st Earl of Callendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Livingston,_1st_Earl_of_Callendar "James Livingston, 1st Earl of Callendar"), sent Baillie across the Ribble to follow the main body just as Langdale, with 3,000 [infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infantry "Infantry") and 500 cavalry, met the first shock of Cromwell's attack on Preston Moor. Hamilton, like Charles at Edgehill, passively shared in, without directing, the [Battle of Preston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Preston_/(1648/) "Battle of Preston (1648)"), and, though Langdale's men fought fiercely, they were driven to the Ribble after four hours' struggle.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191149._Preston_Fight-30) Baillie attempted to cover the Ribble and [Darwen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Darwen "River Darwen") bridges on the Wigan road, but Cromwell had forced his way across both before nightfall. Pursuit was at once undertaken, and not relaxed until Hamilton had been driven through Wigan and [Winwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winwick,_Cheshire "Winwick, Cheshire") to [Uttoxeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uttoxeter "Uttoxeter") and [Ashbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashbourne,_Derbyshire "Ashbourne, Derbyshire"). There, pressed furiously in rear by Cromwell's cavalry and held up in front by the militia of the midlands, the remnant of the Scottish army laid down its arms on 25 August. Various attempts were made to raise the Royalist standard in Wales and elsewhere, but Preston was the death-blow. On 28 August, starving and hopeless of relief, the Colchester Royalists surrendered to Lord Fairfax.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191149._Preston_Fight-30) Execution of Charles I ---------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_English_Civil_War&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Execution of Charles I")\] The victors in the Second Civil War were not merciful to those who had brought war into the land again. On the evening of the surrender of Colchester, [Charles Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lucas "Charles Lucas") and [George Lisle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lisle_/(Royalist/) "George Lisle (Royalist)") were shot. Laugharne, Poyer and Powel were sentenced to death, but Poyer alone was executed on 25 April 1649, being the victim selected by lot. Of five prominent Royalist peers who had fallen into the hands of Parliament, three, the Duke of Hamilton, the Earl of Holland, and Lord [Capel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Capell,_1st_Baron_Capell_of_Hadham "Arthur Capell, 1st Baron Capell of Hadham"), one of the Colchester prisoners, were beheaded at Westminster on 9 March. Above all, after long hesitations, even after renewal of negotiations, the Army and the Independents conducted "[Pride's Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pride%27s_Purge "Pride's Purge")" of the House removing their ill-wishers, and created a court for the trial and sentence of King Charles I.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson191149._Preston_Fight-30) At the end of the trial the [59 Commissioners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_regicides_of_Charles_I "List of regicides of Charles I") (judges) found Charles I guilty of [high treason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_treason "High treason"), as a "tyrant, traitor, murderer and public enemy".[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKelsey2003583%E2%80%93616-31)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKirby1999The_trial_of_King_Charles_I_...-32) He was beheaded on a scaffold in front of the [Banqueting House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banqueting_House "Banqueting House") of the [Palace of Whitehall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Whitehall "Palace of Whitehall") on 30 January 1649. After the [Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration") in 1660, the [regicides who were still alive and not living in exile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_regicides_of_Charles_I "List of regicides of Charles I") were either executed or sentenced to life imprisonment. Capitulation of Pontefract Castle --------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Second_English_Civil_War&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Capitulation of Pontefract Castle")\] [![Image 15](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Pontefract_Castle%2C_2010_%281%29.jpg/250px-Pontefract_Castle%2C_2010_%281%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pontefract_Castle,_2010_/(1/).jpg) Pontefract Castle was [slighted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slighting "Slighting") on the orders of Parliament. [Pontefract Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontefract_Castle "Pontefract Castle") was noted by [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") as "\[...\] one of the strongest inland garrisons in the kingdom".[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDL_staff2012...Historic_Properties...-33) Even in ruins, the castle held out in the north for the Royalists. Upon the execution of Charles I, the garrison recognised [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") as king and refused to surrender. On 24 March 1649, almost two months after Charles was beheaded, the garrison of the last Royalist stronghold finally capitulated. Parliament had the remains of the castle demolished the same year.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWakefield_staff2010History_of_Pontefract_Castle-34)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWakefield_staff2012Pontefract_Castle-35)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELimbird1832Pontefract_Castle-36) Following Charles's execution, the [Commonwealth of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England "Commonwealth of England") was established. In Scotland, [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") became the new king, the resulting tensions leading to the [Anglo-Scottish War of 1650 to
