but many based in England and Ireland | | Casualties and losses | | Total of 28,000 battlefield deaths on both sides, more soldiers die from disease, c. 45,000 civilian deaths, both from disease and deliberate targeting | Between 1639 and 1652, [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Scotland "Kingdom of Scotland") was involved in the [Wars of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Wars of the Three Kingdoms"), a series of conflicts which included the [Bishops' Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops%27_Wars "Bishops' Wars"), the [Irish Rebellion of 1641](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Rebellion_of_1641 "Irish Rebellion of 1641"), the [English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War"), the [Irish Confederate Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Confederate_Wars "Irish Confederate Wars") and finally the [conquest of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromwellian_conquest_of_Ireland "Cromwellian conquest of Ireland") and the [subjugation of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Scottish_war_/(1650%E2%80%931652/) "Anglo-Scottish war (1650–1652)") by the English [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army"). Within Scotland, from 1644 to 1645 a Scottish civil war was fought between Scottish [Royalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier")—supporters of [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") under [James Graham, 1st Marquess of Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_1st_Marquess_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquess of Montrose")—and the [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters"), who had controlled [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") since 1639 and who were allied with [English Parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead"). The Scottish Royalists, aided by Irish troops, had a rapid series of victories in 1644–45, but were eventually defeated by the Covenanters. The Covenanters then found themselves at odds with the English Parliament, so they signed [the Engagement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Engagement_/(1647/) "The Engagement (1647)") with Charles I in 1647 and supported him in the [second English civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_civil_war "Second English civil war"). Following Charles' execution, they received and crowned his son [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") at Scone and thus stated their intention to place him on the thrones of England and Ireland as well. In 1650, Scotland was invaded and occupied by the New Model Army under [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell"). Origins of the war – wars in three kingdoms ------------------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Origins of the war – wars in three kingdoms")\] The war originated in Scottish opposition to religious reforms imposed on the [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland") (_[the Kirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_/(word/) "Kirk (word)"))_ by [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England"). This culminated in February 1638 when representatives from all sections of Scottish society agreed a [National Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Covenant "National Covenant"), pledging resistance to liturgical 'innovations.' An important factor in the political contest with Charles was the Covenanter belief they were preserving an established and divinely ordained form of religion which he was seeking to alter. The Covenant also expressed wider dissatisfaction with the sidelining of Scotland since the [Stuart kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_monarchs "Stuart monarchs") became monarchs of [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") in 1603, while the Kirk was viewed as a symbol of Scottish independence.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMackieLenmanParker1986204%E2%80%93205-1) [![Image 20](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/EDI_CITY_CAC_1978_113.jpg/250px-EDI_CITY_CAC_1978_113.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EDI_CITY_CAC_1978_113.jpg) The Signing of the [National Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Covenant "National Covenant") in [Greyfriars Churchyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greyfriars_Churchyard "Greyfriars Churchyard"), 1638 by [William Hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hole_/(artist/) "William Hole (artist)") Victory in the 1639 and 1640 [Bishops Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops_Wars "Bishops Wars") left the Covenanters firmly in control of Scotland but also destabilised [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Ireland "Kingdom of Ireland") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England"). Widespread opposition to Crown policies meant the [Parliament of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") refused to fund war against the Scots, leading Charles to consider raising an army of Irish Catholics in return for abolishing the [penal laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penal_laws_/(Ireland/) "Penal laws (Ireland)") against them. This prospect alarmed his enemies in both England and Scotland; when the Covenanters threatened to provide military support for their co-religionists in [Ulster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster "Ulster"), it sparked the [Irish Rebellion of 1641](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Rebellion_of_1641 "Irish Rebellion of 1641"), which quickly degenerated into massacres of [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant "Protestant") settlers in Ireland.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2004146%E2%80%93148-2) The Covenanters responded in April 1642 by sending [an army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanter_Army_in_Ireland "Covenanter Army in Ireland") to Ulster led by [Robert Monro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Monro "Robert Monro"), which engaged in equally bloody reprisals against Catholics. Although both Charles and Parliament supported raising troops to suppress the rebellion in Ireland, neither side trusted the other with their control. A struggle for control of military resources ultimately led to the outbreak of the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") in August 1642.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton20035%E2%80%936-3) Scottish Royalists and Covenanters ---------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Scottish Royalists and Covenanters")\] [![Image 21](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg/250px-1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg) [Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_1st_Marquess_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquess of Montrose"); a Covenanter general in 1639 and 1640 who became leader of the Royalist campaign 1644–1645 The [Scottish Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Reformation "Scottish Reformation") established a kirk that was [Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_polity "Presbyterian polity") in structure and [Calvinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinism "Calvinism") in doctrine. By 1640, less than 2% of Scots were Catholics, concentrated in places like [South Uist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Uist "South Uist"), controlled by [Clanranald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clanranald "Clanranald"), but despite its minority status, fear of [popery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Catholicism "Anti-Catholicism") remained widespread.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFissel1994269,_278-4) Since Calvinists believed a 'well-ordered' monarchy was part of God's plan, the Covenanters committed to "defend the king's person and authority with our goods, bodies, and lives" and the idea of government without a king was inconceivable.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacleod20095%E2%80%9319_passim-5) This meant that unlike England, throughout the war all Scots agreed the institution of monarchy itself was divinely ordered and hence why the Covenanters supported the restoration of Charles I in the [Second English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War "Second English Civil War"), then his son in the [Third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_English_Civil_War "Third English Civil War"). Where Covenanters and Scottish Royalists disagreed was the nature and extent of Royal authority versus that of the people, including through the popularly governed Presbyterian church; the relative narrowness of this distinction meant Montrose was not unusual in fighting on both sides.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris201553%E2%80%9354-6) Royalism was most prominent in the [Scottish Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Highlands "Scottish Highlands") and [Aberdeenshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeenshire "Aberdeenshire"), due to a mix of religious, cultural and political reasons; Montrose switched sides because he distrusted Argyll's ambition, fearing he would eventually dominate Scotland and possibly depose the King.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStevenson2004-7) Furthermore, the [Gàidhealtachd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%A0idhealtachd "Gàidhealtachd") was a distinct cultural, political and economic region of Scotland. It was [Gaelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Gaelic_language "Scottish Gaelic language") in language and customs and at this time was largely outside of the control of the Scottish government. Some Highland [clans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clans "Clans") preferred the more distant authority of King Charles to the powerful and well-organised [Lowlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Lowlands "Scottish Lowlands") based government of the Covenanters. Clan politics and feuds also played a role; when the Presbyterian [Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Campbell "Clan Campbell"), led by their chief, [Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll"), sided with the Covenanters, their rivals automatically took the opposing side. It should be said some of these factors overlap that spanned the Irish Sea: for instance, the MacDonalds were Catholics, were sworn enemies of the Campbells, and had a strong [Gaelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaels "Gaels") identity. Historian David Stevenson writes: "It is a moot point whether one should call the MacDonnells of Antrim Scots or Irish... To the MacDonnells themselves the question was largely irrelevant, they had more in common with native Irish and Scots Highlanders, with whom they shared a common Gaelic language and culture than with those who ruled them".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStevenson20058-8) The Irish intervention ---------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: The Irish intervention")\] Montrose had already tried and failed to lead a [Royalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier") uprising by 1644 when he was presented with a ready-made Royalist army. The [Irish Confederates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_Ireland "Confederate Ireland"), who were loosely aligned with the Royalists, agreed in that year to send an expedition to Scotland. From their point of view, this would tie up Scottish Covenanter troops who would otherwise be used in Ireland or England. The Irish sent 1500 men to Scotland under the command of [Alasdair MacColla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alasdair_MacColla "Alasdair MacColla") MacDonald, a MacDonald clansman from the [Western Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Isles "Western Isles") of Scotland. They included [Manus O'Cahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manus_O%27Cahan%27s_Regiment_/(English_Civil_War/) "Manus O'Cahan's Regiment (English Civil War)") (an Irish cousin to MacColla) and his 500-man regiment. Shortly after landing, the Irish linked up with Montrose at [Blair Atholl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blair_Atholl "Blair Atholl") and proceeded to raise forces from the MacDonalds and other anti-Campbell Highland clans. The new Royalist army led by Montrose and MacColla was in some respects very formidable. Its Irish and Highland troops were extremely mobile, marching quickly over long distances – even over the rugged Highland terrain – and were capable of enduring very harsh conditions and poor rations. They did not fight in the massed [pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pike_/(weapon/) "Pike (weapon)") and [musket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musket "Musket") formations that dominated continental Europe at the time, but fired their muskets in loose order before closing with swords and half-pikes. This tactic was effective in such a wilderness and swept away the poorly trained Covenanter militias that were sent against them. These locally raised levies frequently ran away when faced with a terrifying [Highland charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highland_charge "Highland charge"), and were slaughtered as they ran. However, the Royalist army also had major problems: the clans from the west of Scotland could not be persuaded to fight for long away from their homes – seeing their principal enemy as the Campbells rather than the Covenanters, which resulted in fluctuating membership – and the Royalists also lacked [cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalry "Cavalry"), leaving them vulnerable in open country. Montrose overcame some of these disadvantages through his leadership and by taking advantage of the forbidding Highland mountains. Keeping his enemies guessing where he would strike next, Montrose would sally out to attack lowland garrisons and withdraw to the Highlands when threatened by the more numerous enemy. In the safety of the mountains, he could fight on terrain familiar to his army, or lead the Covenanters on wild goose chases.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStevenson2004-7)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWedgwood199867-9) The year of Royalist triumph and collapse ----------------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: The year of Royalist triumph and collapse")\] [![Image 22](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg/250px-The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg) Archibald Campbell, Covenanter and Chief of the Campbell clan From 1644 to 1645 Montrose led the Royalists to six famous victories, defeating covenanting armies larger than his own of roughly 2000 men (except at Kilsyth, where he led approximately 5,000).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStevenson2004-7) In the Autumn of 1644, the Royalists marched across the Highlands to [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth,_Scotland "Perth, Scotland"), where they smashed a Covenanter force at the [Battle of Tippermuir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tippermuir "Battle of Tippermuir") on 1 September. Shortly afterwards, another Covenanter militia met a similar fate [outside Aberdeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Aberdeen_/(1644/) "Battle of Aberdeen (1644)") on 13 September. Unwisely, Montrose let his men pillage Perth and [Aberdeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeen "Aberdeen") after taking them, leading to hostility to his forces in an area where Royalist sympathies had been strong. Following these victories, MacColla insisted on pursuing the MacDonald's war against the Campbells in [Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyll "Argyll") in western Scotland. In December 1644, the Royalists rampaged through the Campbells' country. During the clan warfare [Inveraray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inveraray "Inveraray") was torched and all armed men were put to the sword; approximately 900 Campbells were killed.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTECowan1995176-10) In response to the attack on his clansmen, [Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll") assembled the Campbell clansmen to repel the invaders. Montrose, finding himself trapped in the [Great Glen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Glen "Great Glen") between Argyll and Covenanters advancing from [Inverness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverness "Inverness"), decided on a flanking march through the wintry mountains of [Lochaber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lochaber "Lochaber") and surprised Argyll at the [Battle of Inverlochy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Inverlochy_/(1645/) "Battle of Inverlochy (1645)") (2 February 1645). The Covenanters and Campbells were crushed, with losses of 1,500. Montrose's famous march was acclaimed as "one of the great exploits in the history of British arms" by John Buchan and [C. V. Wedgwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._V._Wedgwood "C. V. Wedgwood").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWedgwood199882-11) The victory at Inverlochy gave the Royalists control over the western Highlands and attracted other clans and noblemen to their cause. The most important of these were the [Gordons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Gordon,_3rd_Marquess_of_Huntly "Lewis Gordon, 3rd Marquess of Huntly"), who provided the Royalists with [cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalry "Cavalry") for the first time. Inverlochy was an important strategic victory for the Royalists, because the Scottish Covenanter army in England was ordered to send a proportion of their force north to help bolster the Covenanter forces in Scotland. This significantly weakened the Scottish army in England and it was only the lack of Royalist infantry and artillery in the north of England that prevented [Prince Rupert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Rupert "Prince Rupert") from attacking them. In April 1645, to hinder the northwards movement of English Royalist field artillery, [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") [led a cavalry raid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War#Cromwell's_raid "First English Civil War") into the English Midlands. The raid was the first active operation carried out by the newly formed [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911P._412_%C2%A7_%22Rupert's_Northern_March%22_and_%22Cromwell's_Raid%22-12) [![Image 23](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Alexleslie.jpg/250px-Alexleslie.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alexleslie.jpg) [Alexander Leslie, 1st Earl of Leven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Leslie,_1st_Earl_of_Leven "Alexander Leslie, 1st Earl of Leven"), Lord General of the Covenanter Army In April Montrose was surprised by [General William Baillie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Baillie_/(soldier/) "William Baillie (soldier)") after a raid on Dundee, but eluded capture by having his troops double back on the coast road and fleeing inland in a corkscrew retreat. Another Covenanter army under [John Urry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Urry_/(soldier/) "John Urry (soldier)") was hastily assembled and sent against the Royalists. At [Auldearn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auldearn "Battle of Auldearn"), near [Nairn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairn "Nairn"), Montrose placed Macdonald and most of the infantry in view of the enemy and concealed the cavalry and remaining infantry. Despite Macdonald attacking prematurely, the ruse worked, and Urry was defeated on 9 May. Another cat-and-mouse game between Bailie and Montrose led to the [Battle of Alford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Alford "Battle of Alford") on 2 July. Montrose confronted the Covenanters after the latter had forded the [Don](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Don,_Aberdeenshire "River Don, Aberdeenshire"), forcing them to fight with the river at their back and on uneven ground. The Royalists triumphed and advanced into the lowlands. Bailie went in pursuit and Montrose waited for him at [Kilsyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kilsyth "Battle of Kilsyth"). During the ensuing battle the Royalists were inadvertently aided by Argyll and other members of the "Committee of Estates," who ordered Bailie to make a flank march across the front of the Royalist army, which pounced on them and triumphed. After Kilsyth (15 August), Montrose seemed to have won control of all Scotland: In late 1645, such prominent towns as [Dundee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dundee "Dundee") and [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow") fell to his forces. The Covenanting government had temporarily collapsed, paying for its over-confidence in defeating Royalist resistance. As the royally commissioned lieutenant-governor and captain-general of Scotland, Montrose used his powers to summon parliament to meet in Glasgow, but the limitations of his triumph soon became clear. King Charles was in no position to join the Royalists in Scotland, and though Montrose wanted to further Royalist objectives by raising troops in the southeast of Scotland and marching on England, MacColla showed that his priorities lay with the war of the MacDonalds against the Campbells and occupied Argyll. The Gordons also returned home, to defend their own lands in the northeast. During his campaign, Montrose had been unable to attract many lowland royalists to his cause. Even after Kilsyth few joined him, having been alienated by his use of Irish Catholic troops, who were "regarded as barbarians as well as enemies of true religion." Additionally, his covenanting past "left lingering mistrust among royalists."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStevenson2004-7) Montrose, his forces having split up, was surprised and defeated by the Covenanters, led by [David Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leslie,_1st_Lord_Newark "David Leslie, 1st Lord Newark"), at the [Battle of Philiphaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Philiphaugh "Battle of Philiphaugh"). Approximately 100 Irish prisoners, having surrendered upon promise of quarter, were executed, and 300 of the Royalist army's camp followers – mostly women and children – were killed in cold blood.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTECowan1995237-13) MacColla retreated to [Kintyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kintyre "Kintyre"), where he held out until the following year. In September 1646 Montrose fled to Norway. The Royalist victories in Scotland had evaporated almost overnight owing to the disunited nature of their forces. The end of the civil war in Scotland ------------------------------------ \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: The end of the civil war in Scotland")\] The [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") had ended in May 1646, when [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") surrendered to the Scottish Covenanter army in England. After failing to persuade the King to take the Covenant, the Scots finally handed him over to the commissioners of the English Parliament (the "[Long Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Parliament "Long Parliament")") in early 1647. At the same time they received part payment for the service of their army in England, which then returned north. In 1646, Montrose left for [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway"), while MacColla returned to Ireland with his remaining Irish and Highland troops to re-join the [Confederates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_Ireland "Confederate Ireland"). Those who had fought for Montrose, particularly the Irish, were massacred by the Covenanters whenever they were captured, in reprisal for the atrocities the Royalists had committed in Argyll. Scotland and the Second Civil War --------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Scotland and the Second Civil War")\] [![Image 24](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Oliver_Cromwell_by_Samuel_Cooper.jpg/250px-Oliver_Cromwell_by_Samuel_Cooper.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Oliver_Cromwell_by_Samuel_Cooper.jpg) [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell"). When the Covenanters' alliance with the English Parliament broke down, Cromwell invaded Scotland and conquered the country Ironically, no sooner had the [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanter "Covenanter") defeated the [Royalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier") at home than they were negotiating with Charles I against the English Parliament. The Covenanters could not get their erstwhile allies to agree on a political and religious settlement to the wars, failing to get [Presbyterianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism "Presbyterianism") established as the official religion in the Three Kingdoms and fearing that the [Parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") would threaten Scottish independence. Many Covenanters feared that under Parliament, "our poor country should be made a province of England." A faction of the Covenanters known as the [Engagers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers "Engagers"), led by the [Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 1st Duke of Hamilton"), therefore [sent an army to England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_invasion_of_England_/(1648/) "Scottish invasion of England (1648)") to try to restore Charles I in 1648. However, it was routed by [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell")'s [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") at the [Battle of Preston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Preston_/(1648/) "Battle of Preston (1648)") and annihilated at the [Battle of Winwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Winwick "Battle of Winwick"). This intervention on behalf of the King caused a brief civil war within the Covenanting movement. The most hardline Presbyterians under the Earl of Argyll rebelled against the main Scottish army under [David Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leslie_/(Scottish_general/) "David Leslie (Scottish general)"). The two factions came to blows at the [Battle of Stirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stirling_/(1648/) "Battle of Stirling (1648)") in September 1648, before a peace was hastily negotiated. Charles was executed by the [Rump Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rump_Parliament "Rump Parliament") in 1649, and Hamilton, who had been captured after Preston, was executed soon after. This left the extreme Covenanters, still led by Argyll, as the main force in the Kingdom. ### Montrose's defeat and death \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Montrose's defeat and death")\] [![Image 25](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Arms_of_Montrose.png/250px-Arms_of_Montrose.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arms_of_Montrose.png) A grisly souvenir of Montrose's hanging: His right arm (seen front and back) and sword In June 1649, [Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_1st_Marquess_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquess of Montrose") was restored by the exiled [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") to the now nominal lieutenancy of Scotland. Charles also opened negotiations with the Covenanters, now dominated by Argyll's radical Presbyterian [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party"). Because Montrose had very little support in the lowlands, Charles was willing to disavow his most consistent supporter to become a king on terms dictated by the Covenanters. In March 1650 Montrose landed in [Orkney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orkney "Orkney") to take the command of a small force, composed mainly of continental mercenaries, which he had sent on before him. Crossing to the mainland, Montrose tried in vain to raise the clans, and on 27 April he was surprised and routed at the [Battle of Carbisdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Carbisdale "Battle of Carbisdale") in Ross-shire. After wandering for some time he was surrendered by [Neil Macleod of Assynt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_MacLeod#17th_century_&_Civil_War "Clan MacLeod"), to whose protection, in ignorance of Macleod's political enmity, he had entrusted himself. He was brought a prisoner to [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh"), and on 20 May sentenced to death by the Parliament. He was [hanged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanging "Hanging") on the 21st, with [Wishart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wishart_/(bishop/) "George Wishart (bishop)")'s laudatory biography of him put round his neck. To the last, he protested that he was a real Covenanter and a loyal subject. Anglo-Scottish war, 1650–1652 ----------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Anglo-Scottish war, 1650–1652")\] Despite their conflict with the Scottish Royalists, the Covenanters then committed themselves to the cause of Charles II, signing the [Treaty of Breda (1650)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Breda_/(1650/) "Treaty of Breda (1650)") with him in the hope of securing an independent Presbyterian Scotland free of Parliamentarian interference. Charles landed in Scotland at [Garmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garmouth "Garmouth") in [Moray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moray "Moray") on 23 June 1650 and signed the 1638 Covenant and the 1643 Solemn League immediately after coming ashore. The threat posed by King Charles II with his new Covenanter allies was considered to be the greatest facing the new English Republic, and [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") left some of his subordinates in Ireland to continue [their conquest of the island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromwellian_conquest_of_Ireland "Cromwellian conquest of Ireland") and returned to England in May. He arrived in Scotland on 22 July 1650, advancing along the east coast towards Edinburgh. By the end of August, his army was reduced by disease and running out of supplies, so he was forced to order a retreat towards his base at the port of Dunbar. A Scottish Covenanter army under the command of [David Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leslie_/(Scottish_general/) "David Leslie (Scottish general)") had been shadowing his progress. Seeing some of Cromwell's sick troops being taken on board the waiting ships, Leslie made ready to attack what he believed was a weakened remnant (though some historians report that he was ordered to fight against his better judgment by the Covenanter General Assembly). Cromwell seized the opportunity, and the [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") inflicted a crushing defeat on the Scots at the subsequent [Battle of Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dunbar_/(1650/) "Battle of Dunbar (1650)") on 3 September. Leslie's army, which had strong ideological ties to the radical [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party"), was destroyed, losing over 14,000 men killed, wounded and taken prisoner. Cromwell's army then took [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") and by the end of the year his army had occupied much of southern Scotland. [![Image 26](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Cromwell_at_Dunbar_Andrew_Carrick_Gow.jpg/250px-Cromwell_at_Dunbar_Andrew_Carrick_Gow.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cromwell_at_Dunbar_Andrew_Carrick_Gow.jpg) _[Cromwell at Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromwell_at_Dunbar "Cromwell at Dunbar")_, by [Andrew Carrick Gow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carrick_Gow "Andrew Carrick Gow"). The Battle of Dunbar was a crushing defeat for the Covenanters This military disaster discredited the radical Covenanters known as the [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party") and caused the Covenanters and Scottish Royalists to bury their differences (at least temporarily) to try to repel Cromwell's invasion of Scotland. The Scottish Parliament passed the Act of Levy in December 1650, requiring every burgh and shire to raise a quota of soldiers. A new round of conscription was undertaken, both in the Highlands and the Lowlands, to form a truly national army named the Army of the Kingdom, that was put under the command of Charles II himself. Although this was the largest force put into the field by the Scots during the Wars, it was badly trained and its morale was low as many of its constituent Royalist and Covenanter parts had until recently been fighting each other. In July 1651, under the command of General John Lambert, part of Cromwell's force crossed the [Firth of Forth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firth_of_Forth "Firth of Forth") into [Fife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fife "Fife") and defeated the Scots at the [Battle of Inverkeithing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Inverkeithing "Battle of Inverkeithing"). The New Model Army advanced towards the royal base at [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth,_Scotland "Perth, Scotland"). In danger of being outflanked, Charles ordered his army south into England in a desperate last-ditch attempt to evade Cromwell and spark a Royalist uprising there. Cromwell followed Charles into England leaving [George Monck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Monck "George Monck") to finish the campaign in Scotland. Meanwhile, Monck took [Stirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling "Stirling") on 14 August and [Dundee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dundee "Dundee") on 1 September, reportedly killing up to 2,000 of its 12,000 population and destroying every ship in the city's harbour, 60 in total. The Scottish Army of the Kingdom marched towards the west of England because it was in that area that English Royalist sympathies were strongest. However, although some English Royalists joined the army, they came in far fewer numbers than Charles and his Scottish supporters had hoped. Cromwell finally engaged the new king at [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Worcester "Battle of Worcester") on 3 September 1651, and beat him – in the process all but wiping out his army, killing 3,000 and taking 10,000 prisoners. Many of the Scottish prisoners taken by Cromwell were sold into indentured labour in the West Indies, Virginia and [Berwick, Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berwick,_Maine "Berwick, Maine"). This defeat marked the real end of the Scottish war effort. Charles escaped to the European continent and with his flight, the Covenanters' hopes for resisting Cromwell's invasion were dashed. From occupation to Restoration ------------------------------ \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: From occupation to Restoration")\] [![Image 27](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/General_Monck.jpg/250px-General_Monck.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:General_Monck.jpg) General Monck commanded the Parliamentarian forces that occupied Scotland during the Interregnum and led his troops to London to restore the monarchy in 1660 Between 1651 and 1654, a Royalist rising took place in Scotland.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker20052-14) [Dunnottar Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunnottar_Castle "Dunnottar Castle") was the last stronghold to fall to Parliamentarian troops in May 1652. Under the terms of the [Tender of Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tender_of_Union "Tender of Union"), the Scots were given 30 seats in a united Parliament in London, with General Monck appointed as the military governor of Scotland. His troops continued to garrison Scotland for the rest of the [Interregnum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interregnum_/(England/) "Interregnum (England)"). Sporadic Royalist rebellions continued throughout the Commonwealth period in Scotland, particularly in the western Highlands, where [Alasdair MacColla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alasdair_MacColla "Alasdair MacColla") had raised his forces in the 1640s. The northwest Highlands was the scene of another pro-Royalist uprising in 1653–55, which was only put down with the deployment of 6,000 New Model Army troops there. Monck garrisoned forts all over the Highlands – for example at [Inverness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverness "Inverness"), and finally put an end to Royalist resistance when he began deporting prisoners to the [West Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Indies "West Indies") as [indentured labourers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indentured_labour "Indentured labour"). However, lawlessness remained a problem, with bandits known as [mosstroopers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosstroopers "Mosstroopers"), very often former Royalist or Covenanter soldiers, attacking both Parliamentarian troops and Scottish civilians. After the death of Oliver Cromwell in 1658, the factions and divisions which had struggled for supremacy during the early years of the interregnum reemerged. Monck, who had served Cromwell and the English Parliament throughout the civil wars, judged that his best interests and those of his country lay in the Restoration of Charles II. In 1660, he marched his troops south from Scotland to ensure the monarchy's reinstatement. Scotland's Parliament and legislative autonomy were restored under [The Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restoration_/(Scotland/) "Restoration (Scotland)") though many issues that had led to the wars; religion, Scotland's form of government and the status of the Highlands, remained unresolved. After the [Glorious Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glorious_Revolution "Glorious Revolution") of 1688, many more Scots would die over the same disputes in [Jacobite rebellions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobite_rebellions "Jacobite rebellions"). It is estimated that roughly 28,000 men were killed in combat in Scotland itself during the Wars of the Three Kingdoms. More soldiers usually died of disease than in action at this time (the ratio was often 3–1), so it is reasonable to speculate that the true military death toll is higher than this figure. In addition, it is estimated that around 15,000 civilians died as a direct result of the war – either through massacres or by disease. More indirectly, another 30,000 people died of the [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandemic "Pandemic") in Scotland between 1645 and 1649, a disease that was partly spread by the movement of armies throughout the country. If we also take into account the thousands of Scottish troops who died in the civil wars in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War") and [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Confederate_Wars "Irish Confederate Wars") (another 20,000 soldiers at least), the [Wars of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Wars of the Three Kingdoms") certainly represent one of the bloodiest episodes in Scottish history. 1648 and All That
=================

The Scottish Invasions of England, 1648 and 1651. Proceedings of the 2022 Helion and Company Century of the Soldier Conference

**Series** : [Century of the Soldier 1618-1721](https://www.helion.co.uk/series/century-of-the-soldier-1618-1721.php) #101

**Editor** : [Charles Singleton](https://www.helion.co.uk/people/charles-singleton.php)

![Image 6: 1648 and All That : The Scottish Invasions of England, 1648 and 1651. Proceedings of the 2022 Helion and Company Century of the Soldier Conference](https://www.helion.co.uk/images/books/i2/helion1001410.jpg.pagespeed.ce.Vz8HY0Vu1U.jpg)

Print Editions
--------------

### Paperback

£25.00 FREE UK delivery on orders over £30

Despatched within 6-9 working days

Details
-------

**General** - Pages : 122 | Images : 9 b/w illustrations, 8 b/w photos, 7 maps, 6 tables

**Paperback** - Date of Publication : 6th April 2023 | Size : 248mm x 180mm | ISBN : 9781804513644 | Helion Book Code : HEL1771

The resumption of conflict between 1648 and 1651 is frequently referred to as the Second and Third Civil Wars. The period marked not only a return to war, but to a bloodier, more violent conflict that had perhaps been seen before in the British Isles. Massacre, summary executions, wonton destruction and assault on the civilian population were commonplace. In early 1648 a political faction called the ‘Engagers’ gained control of the Scottish Government and sent an army into England to support numerous pro-Royalist risings across the country. Poorly equipped and trained with low morale, the Scottish ‘Engager’ Army and its Royalist allies were no match for the New Model Army led by Cromwell. The two sides met at Preston in August 1648 and after an initial clash, the Scots finally surrendered at Warrington two days later.

Following the execution of Charles Ist in January 1649, the Scots supporting his son Charles IInd went to war against England, now a republic. A second invasion of England was launched, and the Scots found themselves corned at Worcester by English forces, once again led by Oliver Cromwell. The battle, the last major action of the British Civil Wars was fought on the 3rd September 1651, was described by Cromwell as ‘a crowning mercy’.

The venue for the 2022 conference was Worcester Cathedral. The obvious theme for the conference was the Scottish invasions of England in 1648 and 1651. Not only did Worcester witness the last major battle of the British Civil Wars, but the Cathedral was used as a temporary prison to hold the Scottish prisoners.

The papers in this book of proceedings include

Ronald Hutton – Key Note Speaker and Foreword

Stuart Jennings – Colonel Francis Thornhagh and the Battle of Preston, 1648

Peter Gaunt – A Tale of Two Risings: Was the second civil war in England and Wales

primarily pro-Royalist or anti-Parliamentarian?

Malcolm Wanklyn – The Control of Command in the British Wars 1642-1651

Edward Furgol – Three armies into one? Scottish Engager military organisation in 1648
